title: Locking: from locks to correct schedules
lead: The previous lesson detected bad interleavings after seeing a schedule. Now an order update arrives one operation at a time. We need rules that stop unsafe access before it happens, and a way to resolve the waiting those rules create.
goals: Simulate shared/exclusive locks and the two locking phases
Handle deadlocks through detection or timestamp-based prevention

sections.title: Let readers share, but protect an update
sections.html:
Two clerks can read the same order without changing it. If one is changing its quantity, however, another reader should not use a half-finished update. A lock manager tracks which transaction holds permission on each object and which requests are waiting.

An S lock grants shared read permission; an X lock grants exclusive read/write permission. Compatibility is between different transactions:

Held / requestedSX
SGrant togetherWait
XWaitWait

Request the appropriate lock before accessing an object. A reader that later wants to write requests an upgrade from S to X. Its own S lock does not block itself, but another reader's S lock prevents that upgrade.

Permission for each access is not enough. Suppose T1 locks X(A), writes, unlocks; T2 locks X(A), writes, unlocks; T1 then locks S(A) and reads. All accesses held a suitable lock, yet the writes impose T1→T2 and the later read imposes T2→T1.

The missing rule is two-phase locking (2PL). During growing, acquire or upgrade locks. The first release begins shrinking: only releases are permitted afterward. Thus T1's final acquisition is forbidden. The DBMS can enforce this as requests arrive without knowing all future queries. With properly protected accesses, 2PL guarantees conflict-serializable schedules, while excluding some schedules that could have been serializable.

Basic 2PL may release locks before commit. The lecture's strict 2PL instead retains all S and X locks until transaction completion. Some books call that rigorous 2PL; use the stated convention.

Key takeaway

The first lock release is the phase boundary in 2PL. A transaction cannot return to acquiring locks afterward. The lecture's strict variant additionally delays every release until transaction completion.

T1 and T2 both hold S(A). Can T1 immediately upgrade to X(A)?

Worked answer. No. T2’s S(A) is incompatible with T1’s requested X(A). T1 must wait, and the upgrade must still occur before T1’s first release. Lock compatibility and phase legality are two separate checks.

sections.title: Follow an order update and the reader it blocks
sections.html:
Original example: T1 changes Order.quantity from 2 to 3 and Stock.available from 8 to 7. T2 wants to display the order. Under the lecture's strict 2PL convention:

StepLocks held by T1T2 and data
1X(Order)T1 writes quantity=3; not yet committed
2X(Order)T2 requests S(Order): waits; reads nothing
3X(Order), X(Stock)T1 writes available=7
4None after completionT1 commits and releases; T2 may read quantity=3

If T1 aborts at step 3 instead, restore quantity=2 and available=8 before releasing its protection. T2 then reads 2. It never has to retract an answer based on 3, because it never saw that uncommitted value.

Why wait until completion?

Basic 2PL permits a different ending: T1 has acquired every lock it will need, writes quantity=3, then releases Order while retaining Stock. T2 reads 3 and calculates Invoice=30. If T1 later aborts, T2's invoice has a false premise and must also be undone. This is a cascading abort; a third transaction reading T2's uncommitted invoice extends the chain.

Keeping the update lock prevents the first dirty dependency. The cost is waiting: a long-running transaction holds up conflicting work. The benefit is easier abort handling and the absence of cascading aborts. Correct serialization and safe abort handling are related, but basic 2PL alone gives only the former guarantee.

Is X(Order), update, unlock(Order), X(Stock) valid 2PL? How would you repair it?

Worked answer. No: requesting X(Stock) after the first release re-enters growing. Acquire X(Stock) before any release. Under the lecture’s strict variant, retain both locks until commit or abort finishes.

Sources and teaching scope

Sources: PDF pages 3–17.

sections.title: The safe locks can still leave everyone waiting
sections.html:
T1 holds X(Order). T2 holds X(Stock). Now T1 requests X(Stock), and T2 requests X(Order). Neither can finish its work and release what the other needs.

RequestCurrent holderWaits-for edge
T1 requests StockT2T1 → T2
T2 requests OrderT1T2 → T1

This cycle is a deadlock. A waits-for graph has transactions as nodes and an edge from a blocked requester to its holder. It describes current waiting. The precedence graph in Lecture 19 instead records the order of already executed conflicting operations. A deadlock is not evidence that strict 2PL has permitted a nonserializable execution: the blocked accesses have not happened.

With detection, the DBMS periodically checks the waiting graph. Choose T2 as a victim, roll back its changes, release its locks, and T1 can acquire Stock. Victim choice considers rollback work, locks, dependent transactions, age and previous restarts. Always aborting the same unlucky transaction risks starvation. Frequent checking spends more CPU; rare checking prolongs blocked time.

Another approach prevents hold-and-wait: declare the required set {Order,Stock} and grant the entire set atomically, or grant none. This conservative/preclaiming 2PL requires knowing future locks and can reduce concurrency. Merely requesting the two locks one by one at the beginning still allows T1 and T2 to each hold one, so does not remove the problem.

Key takeaway

Waits-for graphs and precedence graphs answer different questions. A waits-for graph records who is waiting for whom to detect deadlock. A precedence graph records the order of conflicting operations to check conflict serializability.

T1→T2 and T2→T3 are the only waits-for edges. Must someone be aborted?

Worked answer. These edges alone contain no cycle. T3 may finish and release locks, letting T2 and then T1 proceed. Waiting is not automatically deadlock; aborting someone solely for these edges would be unnecessary for cycle removal.

Sources and teaching scope

sections.title: Use transaction age to forbid a waiting cycle
sections.html:
Instead of building a cycle then breaking it, constrain every waiting edge as it is created. Assign timestamps: O=10, M=20, Y=30. Smaller means older; keep that timestamp if a transaction restarts.

Requester and holderWait-dieWound-wait
O requests a lock held by YO waitsAbort Y, then grant when safe
Y requests a lock held by OAbort YY waits

In wait-die, an older requester may wait for a younger holder. A younger requester aborts rather than waiting for an older holder. Every permitted arrow increases timestamp: 10→20→30 is possible, but 30→10 is forbidden. A strictly increasing chain cannot return to 10.

In wound-wait, an older requester forces a younger holder to abort; a younger requester may wait for an older holder. Every waiting arrow decreases: 30→20→10 is possible, but 10→30 is forbidden. Again a cycle is impossible. “Wound” affects the holder; “die” affects the requester. Confusing these roles reverses the rule.

Restart with the original timestamp so a repeatedly aborted transaction does not become youngest again on every retry. It eventually has priority over newer work under the protocol's progress assumptions. Preventing deadlocks does not mean no aborts or no waits: the rules deliberately use both to exclude cycles.

Under wait-die, can waiting edges 10→20, 20→30 and 30→10 all exist?

Worked answer. No. The first two obey old-waits-for-young; the third has a younger requester waiting for an older holder, so timestamp 30 must abort. Under wound-wait the first two would instead be disallowed as waiting edges.

sections.title: Try the protocol on an unfamiliar trace
sections.html:
Before reading the answer, mark the phase boundary in this original trace: T1 acquires S(A), acquires S(B), releases S(A), then requests an upgrade S(B)→X(B). The first release is the boundary. The upgrade is a new, stronger permission after that boundary, so basic 2PL rejects it even though T1 already held B.

Repair it by requesting the upgrade before releasing A. If another transaction holds S(B), wait for compatibility; phase legality does not override other holders. Under strict 2PL, retain A and B until completion rather than releasing A early.

Now two transactions each hold S(A), and both request X(A). Each waits for the other's S lock. This is an upgrade deadlock, so a waits-for detector can find T1↔T2 even though there is only one data object. Resolving it requires choosing a victim or applying a prevention rule; neither reader can simply ignore the other's lock.

Use two separate questions whenever evaluating a proposal: can it expose a bad execution, and can work stop progressing? Strict 2PL protects conflict serializability and avoids cascading aborts under the lecture convention. Deadlock detection or prevention handles progress. Holding locks longer trades some concurrency for easier reasoning; it does not solve every waiting problem.

A teammate says strict 2PL removes deadlocks because locks are released only at the end. Give a concrete counterexample.

Worked answer. T1 holds X(A) and requests X(B); T2 holds X(B) and requests X(A). Both obey the strict retention rule, but neither can reach the end. The waits-for cycle still needs detection or prevention.

quiz.question: T_old requests a lock held by T_new. What does wound-wait do?
options: T_new aborts and releases its locks
quiz.explanation: Under wound-wait, a transaction with a smaller timestamp can force a younger transaction holding the requested lock to abort.
